implementation_notes: The JMS API contains the pattern as a header: the requestor creates a TemporaryQueue with its Session, calls setJMSReplyTo(replyQueue), sends, and receives the reply from that destination; the replier reads getJMSReplyTo() and produces the answer there, copying the message id into JMSCorrelationID. This is the realization shown in the EIP book's JMS example and the standard choice when the broker speaks JMS; when the broker is AMQP-based inside Spring, the template variant hides the address entirely.

variants.name: JMS/Jakarta Messaging JMSReplyTo on a TemporaryQueue
variants.implementation_notes: The JMS API contains the pattern as a header: the requestor creates a TemporaryQueue with its Session, calls setJMSReplyTo(replyQueue), sends, and receives the reply from that destination; the replier reads getJMSReplyTo() and produces the answer there, copying the message id into JMSCorrelationID. This is the realization shown in the EIP book's JMS example and the standard choice when the broker speaks JMS; when the broker is AMQP-based inside Spring, the template variant hides the address entirely.
pitfalls: A TemporaryQueue is owned by the Session that created it: closing or recycling the session (connection pooling!) destroys the address while replies are still in flight.
JMSReplyTo values are provider-specific serializations of a destination, not portable broker-neutral names — never persist them as a contract.
receive() without a timeout blocks the calling thread forever; always pass one and handle the no-reply case.

variants.name: Spring AMQP send-and-receive with direct reply-to
variants.implementation_notes: Spring AMQP turns the pattern into a template call: convertSendAndReceive publishes the request with reply_to pointing at RabbitMQ's amq.rabbitmq.reply-to pseudo queue and consumes the reply on a dedicated listener container, so application code never sees an address. setReplyAddress plus setUseDirectReplyToContainer(false) switch to a fixed reply queue, setReplyTimeout (about five seconds by default) bounds the wait. Prefer this variant inside Spring applications and the JMS variant when the address must be visible, per-request or persisted.
pitfalls: The direct reply-to consumer is shared per template: concurrent callers are matched by correlation id, and a timeout returns null instead of throwing.
Direct reply-to requires the listener container to be running; disabling it without setting a reply address publishes requests whose reply_to nobody consumes.
A fixed reply queue reintroduces stale-message risk: unconsumed replies from earlier runs stay in it until something reads them.
A TemporaryQueue is owned by the Session that created it: closing or recycling the session (connection pooling!) destroys the address while replies are still in flight.
JMSReplyTo values are provider-specific serializations of a destination, not portable broker-neutral names — never persist them as a contract.
receive() without a timeout blocks the calling thread forever; always pass one and handle the no-reply case.
